_about: English texts for the Classic sounds library. Numbers come from Idea/patches.json (left unchanged); this file only holds the translated words, keyed by patch id. Param notes are keyed 'moduleId.jsonParam'.

i-feel-love-bass.title: I Feel Love – sequencer bass
goals: Program a step sequencer with rest steps
A filter envelope for a percussive bass
A tempo-synced delay fills the gaps between the notes (the "gallop")
history: Moroder built almost the whole song on the Moog modular: bass, snare and hi-hats.
The Moog kept drifting out of tune, so it was recorded in pieces of 20–30 seconds.
The bassline only got its typical sound in the mix, through a delay.
gear: Moog modular (borrowed from Eberhard Schoener, operated by Robby Wedel)
tutorial: Sequencer at 8 steps and 125 BPM, with steps 2, 4, 6 and 8 switched off.
The sequencer's Pitch goes to the oscillator, its Gate to both envelopes.
A saw through the low-pass filter. The short filter envelope makes every note "plop".
The VCA output goes into the delay. At 1/16 the repeats fill the rests.

notes.seq.pitchSet: In an interview Moroder mentions "two Cs, a G and a B" (in German note names "B" is B flat). The order of the steps is up to you.
notes.delay.sync: 1/16 at 125 BPM = 120 ms. It lands exactly between the eighth notes and makes the gallop.
notes.out.pan: Computer Music routes the delay to the right main output.

inApp: The delay time is set from the tempo: 1/16 at 125 BPM = 120 ms.
The order of the four notes is a starting point; the source does not give the original order.
Stereo panning from the source (output to the right) is left out: the app plays in the middle.
The two envelopes reach the filter and the VCA directly; the filter's envelope amount is the VCF CV Amt knob.

oxygene-iv-lead.title: Oxygène IV – lead
goals: Two slightly detuned oscillators for a beating sound
An LFO as a subtle vibrato on the pitch
Very long release times: the sound reacts to how long you hold the notes
An effect chain: spring reverb before delay
history: Recorded at home in Jarre's kitchen, with tracks layered on an 8-track recorder.
Processed mainly with tape echo and guitar pedals.
It reached number 4 in the UK singles chart.
tutorial: Two saw oscillators at 32' (two octaves down), detuned slightly against each other. Listen to the beating.
A little LFO on both oscillators: a subtle vibrato.
The filter is almost closed (about 30 Hz) and the envelope opens it. The release lasts over 7 seconds.
Play short and long notes: the sound changes with how long you hold them.
Spring reverb and delay: start dry, then mix them in slowly.

notes.lfo.depth: Source: turn the FM knob up only slightly.
notes.reverb.mix: Source: start dry, then to taste.

inApp: 32' (two octaves down) is Octave −2 on the VCO.
The Reverb uses its Spring type, a model of a spring reverb.
Panning to the left output is left out: the app plays in the middle.
The filter envelope can open the cutoff by up to six octaves here; the source turns it almost fully up.

blade-runner-brass.title: Blade Runner – brass
goals: High-pass and low-pass filter in series
Two envelopes on the same filter cutoff
A big reverb as part of the sound
history: The brass sound itself is simple. It lives from Vangelis' playing and lots of reverb.
From 1980 Vangelis used a Lexicon 224 as his reverb.
tutorial: Two saws, one an octave lower, both detuned slightly against each other.
High-pass first, then low-pass: the high-pass takes away the boom, the low-pass shapes the brass tone.
Two envelopes on the cutoff: a slow, gentle one and a fast, full one for the "blow".
Chorus and lots of reverb. Play the pitch and the cutoff live.

notes.vco1.fineCents: Fathom CM pitch fine -0.03, detune on.
notes.hpf.cutoffHz: Fathom CM cutoff about 600; the unit is unclear.

inApp: Plays up to 8 notes at once, like the CS-80: the Keyboard's Voices knob is at 8, and every module behind it is copied once per voice.
Both envelopes reach the cutoff through a Mixer, because every input takes only one cable. The Mixer levels are the envelope amounts from the source.
Playing pitch and cutoff live with a ribbon, mod wheel or aftertouch is not available.

stranger-things-arp.title: Stranger Things – intro arpeggio
goals: An arpeggiator over a held chord
A random LFO on the pitch for "analog" drift
A filter envelope without sustain for plucked notes
history: Accounts differ on the arpeggio. Roland, quoting Michael Stein, says he played it by hand on an old Oberheim and that the rolling bassline came from a Roland SH-2; tutorials such as Mixdown's credit the arpeggiated line to the SH-2.
The lead is a Roland Jupiter-8; about 25 synthesizers were used for the theme.
tutorial: A held C major 7 chord, the arpeggiator on Down-Up with Hold. Start 2 lets the line begin on G.
Two square oscillators, one an octave lower, plus a sub oscillator.
Two slow random LFOs on the pitch: the notes drift like on an old analog synth.
Filter and amp envelope without sustain: every note dies away.
Open the cutoff slowly by hand, as in the intro.

notes.vcf.cutoffHz: Source: the cutoff is moved by hand during the piece, so try it live.
notes.chorus.mix: Source: chorus is a big part of the 80s sound.

inApp: The Arp starts with the stored C major 7 chord. Hold your own chord on the keys to replace it.
The sub oscillator is a third VCO, one octave below the lower oscillator.
Unison (two voices per note) and filter drive are left out.

sources.title: Roland Articles: the synths of the Stranger Things theme (quotes Michael Stein)

dx7-epiano-1.title: DX7 E.PIANO 1
dx7-epiano-1.artist: Yamaha factory preset (Twin Peaks theme and many 80s ballads)
goals: FM synthesis: carriers and modulators
Algorithm 5: three pairs of modulator → carrier
A high frequency ratio (14) makes the bell-like attack
Velocity sensitivity of the modulators makes the sound respond to touch
history: Factory preset 11 of the DX7, seen as the best-known synth preset of the 80s.

According to a study (Lavengood, 2019, Journal of Popular Music Studies) it was on 61% of the 1986 R&B number-one hits, 40% of the country number-one hits and 39% of the Billboard Hot 100 number-one hits.
On several Whitney Houston songs it is disputed whether you hear a DX7, a modified Rhodes or both.
tutorial: Only operators 1 and 2: ratio 14 on the modulator makes the metallic "tine" attack.
Add operators 3 and 4: the second pair gives the warm body.
Add operators 5 and 6: the ±7 detune makes beating and width.
Play soft and loud: the modulators react strongly to velocity.
Chorus behind it: the typical 80s shine.
inApp: The real preset uses 6 operators. The DX7 E-Piano guide builds 4 of them: two modulator → carrier pairs (ratio 14 for the tine, ratio 1 for the body), played with 4 voices, with chorus and reverb.
A full 6-operator FM module is a possible later step.

on-the-run-sequence.title: On the Run – sequence
goals: Drive a sequencer from a Clock to play sixteenth notes
A resonant filter that sweeps slowly by itself (LFO on the cutoff)
A hi-hat made of white noise and a ring modulator
history: On the Run is the third track of The Dark Side of the Moon (1973).
The eight-note sequence was typed into the sequencer of an EMS Synthi AKS and sped up. Alan Parsons remembered the notes being entered slowly and played back fast.
The sequence runs at 165 BPM while the filter frequency and resonance change.
The hi-hat came from the same synthesizer: white noise into the ring modulator, opened by the sequencer's trigger pulse.
gear: EMS Synthi AKS (the portable VCS3 in a case, with a built-in keyboard and sequencer)
EMS VCS3 (credited on the album, used for the passing-vehicle sounds)
inApp: This patch is our own recreation: the source data has no settings for this sound. Only the tempo and the way the hi-hat is made come from a source; every other knob is marked ≈.
The notes E–G–A–G–D–C–D–E come from transcriptions by ear. Sources disagree about the exact notes, so treat them as a close guess.
The steps are sixteenth notes: a Clock at 165 BPM in 1/16 drives the Sequencer.
Only the filter frequency moves here: this app has no input to sweep the resonance.
Left out: the passing-vehicle sounds, footsteps, voices and the other tape effects of the track.

tutorial.text: A Clock at 165 BPM in sixteenths drives the Sequencer: one step per pulse.
Eight notes, E–G–A–G–D–C–D–E, on a square wave one octave down.
A steep low-pass filter with high resonance. A very slow LFO sweeps its cutoff, so the line keeps changing colour.
The hi-hat: white noise times a very short envelope, in the Ring modulator. Every step ticks.
Synth and hi-hat meet in the Mixer and get a little spring reverb, like the one built into the Synthi.

references: On the Run & FM synthesis (patch in the thread)

sources.title: On the Run (instrumental) – Wikipedia (tempo and hi-hat cite Guesdon & Margotin, Pink Floyd All the Songs, 2017)
Shimamura: EMS VCS3 & Synthi AKS (Japanese; notes by ear)

notes.seq.s1: Notes E–G–A–G–D–C–D–E, from a low E up to the E one octave higher, transcribed by ear; sources disagree.
notes.clk.div: Sixteenth notes: inferred from listening, no source gives the note length.
notes.vco.wave: Square: two recreations (by ear) use a square or 50 % pulse wave.
notes.vcf.res: High resonance: the sources say the resonance was turned during the track; this app cannot sweep it.
notes.lfo.rate: A very slow sweep stands in for the hand-turned filter knob.

tour-de-france.title: Tour de France
facts: The VCV Rack recreation uses Plaits, Bogaudio FM, VCV Fundamental oscillators and filters, drum synthesis and a Chronoblob2 delay.
references: SATURATA MODULAR (patch and MIDI files via Patreon)
